records.name: Dominican Republic
records.summary:
The Dominican Republic demands real caution from trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, and the 2024 Constitutional Court review of the remaining sodomy-law articles (210/260, which applied to police and armed-forces members) has resolved: the current criminal code does not prohibit same-sex relations — though the existence of these articles revealed the institutional culture. There is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination law covering SOGI (Brazil, a foreign government, formally recommended one at the 2024 UPR review), and documented violence against trans women is high, particularly affecting the most marginalised.

Tourist zones (Punta Cana, Puerto Plata) are heavily insulated resort enclaves with international norms; Santo Domingo, the capital, has a visible community and annual Pride caravan. Outside those bubbles, machista culture, police harassment of trans women (especially sex workers), and anti-Haitian (xenophobic) dynamics that compound for dark-skinned trans people are documented.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (30 Aug 2024): documented the Constitutional Court challenge to sodomy-law remnants reaching only police and military officers (no equivalent for heterosexual acts), with HRW's amicus brief arguing equality/privacy violations. SUPERSEDED per resolved review: The 2024 constitutional review of the sodomy-law remnants is resolved: the current criminal code does not prohibit same-sex relations; still no anti-discrimination or marriage recognition.

UPR database (Sexual Rights Initiative): the Dominican Republic accepted recommendations on intersex persons' rights and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity — an accepted international-commitment record with no domestic implementation detail shown.

Time/Amnesty International (31 Mar 2019): TDOV conversation with two activists including Nairovi Castillo of the Dominican Republic, executive director of COTRAVETD (Community of Dominican Trans and Transvestite Sex Workers, co-founded 2004) — first-hand account of trans struggles in the country.

Washington Blade (1 Apr 2017): 300+ activists from Latin America and the Caribbean attended an LGBT/intersex political-engagement conference in Santo Domingo with Dominican government officials speaking — a marker of official-level engagement in 2017.

Washington Blade (27 Apr 2016): documents the backlash against openly gay US Ambassador James 'Wally' Brewster after his June 2015 presentation with his husband in Santo Domingo — framed as attacks on LGBT Dominicans, showing organised domestic opposition climate.

Washington Blade (3 Apr 2017): the openly gay US ambassador's departure left an advocacy void after two years of visible presence (spoke at Santo Domingo Pride, 3 Jul 2016) — trailing marker of the polarised climate his tenure exposed.

records.name: Canada
records.summary:
Canada is exceptionally safe for trans visitors — the strongest of the large Western countries. Gender identity and expression are protected grounds in the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Criminal Code’s hate-crime provisions (Bill C-16, 2017); most provinces offer self-declaration legal gender recognition; federal documents offer an X marker; and healthcare coverage is universal. There are no bathroom laws, no border friction (Canadian authorities have not issued or received trans-traveller warnings), and courts consistently enforce protections.

The counterweights are real but climate-level: police-reported hate crimes have risen six consecutive years (+169% since 2018), with gender identity/expression crimes among the fastest-growing categories; Egale documents a rising organised anti-trans movement; and Alberta/Saskatchewan have enacted resident-facing policy rollbacks (school pronoun and healthcare restrictions). A 2022 federal survey found 39% of 2SLGBTQI+ respondents experienced identity-based violence in five years — 90% of it verbal abuse, 17% physical.

Egale Canada UPR submission (2012): overview of LGBT human rights in Canada - sexual orientation in the Charter since 1995, marriage equality 2005; but trans protections limited and varying by jurisdiction, with no federal gender-identity discrimination law at the time; identifies gaps against the Yogyakarta Principles.

CBC News (Apr 2016): Prince Edward Island amended its Vital Statistics Act so a trans person changes the gender on official documents by declaring their identified gender plus a doctor's letter — the prior surgery requirement removed. A practical document-update pathway in one province.

The Globe and Mail (Jun 2017): the Senate passed Bill C-16 by 67-11, prohibiting discrimination based on gender identity and gender expression and adding gender identity/expression to the Criminal Code hate-motivation provisions — framed as Canadian leadership amid a global anti-LGBT backlash.

Ontario Human Rights Commission policy (Part I): lays out the legal context, case law and legislation for sexual-orientation discrimination complaints under the Ontario Human Rights Code, which expressly covers gender identity and gender expression — official Ontario guidance a visitor/resident can invoke for discrimination recourse.

records.name: Australia
records.summary:
Australia is exceptionally safe for trans visitors. Gender identity has been a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court’s landmark Tickle v Giggle ruling confirmed that gender-identity discrimination protection covers trans women as women — with compensation awarded. States have modernised rapidly: Queensland strengthened discrimination and vilification protections (April 2024) and NSW, another state, passed the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024. There are no bathroom laws and no border friction; and marriage equality has held since 2017 (relevant to same-sex partners travelling together).

Counterweights: the Tickle case itself arose from organised exclusionary activism, which is vocal in Australia; ANROWS research documents systemic discrimination and harassment of trans people; and a NSW court granted a trans woman an apprehended-violence order against a Binary Australia activist who had targeted her — real harassment, but also functioning legal recourse.

ANROWS research briefing: maps current and emerging threats to trans and gender diverse rights in Australia — organised exclusionary campaigns, facilities and records-access disputes, rights-rollback pressures: the live opposition landscape a trans visitor moves through despite strong statutes.

Queensland Parliamentary Library research brief (2003) 'Protecting Transgender Rights under Queensland's Discrimination Law Amendment Act 2002': introduced 'gender identity' as a protected attribute; documents trans people's difficulties with sex designations on passports, licences and birth certificates, high job-loss rates around transition, and greater exposure to assault and harassment in public places.

Organisation Intersex International Australia briefing: argues intersex is not a gender identity and warns against folding intersex into SOGI legal frameworks (recommends SOGIESC terminology) — relevant to how Australian gender-diversity protections are scoped.

Australian Lesbian & Gay Archives, 'Towards Homosexual Equality in Australian Criminal Law - A Brief History' (Carbery, 2nd ed. 2014): state-by-state history of decriminalisation, from British-inherited buggery laws (death penalty in Victoria until 1949) through reform - historical legal context for Australia's current framework.

records.name: New Zealand
records.summary:
New Zealand is exceptionally safe for trans visitors. Legal gender recognition by self-declaration has been in force since 2023 (Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Act); the Law Commission reviewed Human Rights Act protections for trans, non-binary and intersex people in 2024; and takatāpui/rainbow communities have deep institutional recognition. There are no bathroom laws and no border friction.

The counterweights are documented and significant for the street climate: reports of gender-identity hate crimes jumped 42% between 2022 and 2023 (161 to 229 incidents), spiking around the Posie Parker visit (the visiting campaigner); the national survey (Counting Ourselves) found almost 1 in 5 trans and non-binary people were threatened with physical violence in four years, and 8% experienced it; and community advocates accuse police of failing rainbow communities amid far-right agitation (library events crashed, church arson threats).

sources.summary: RNZ (17 Apr 2024), Official Information Act data: 229 gender-identity-motivated hate incidents reported to police in 2023 vs 161 in 2022 — a 42% rise — with police saying the figure likely understates true anti-trans hate, and a spike in the month anti-trans activist Posie Parker visited (March 2023). For this record: the quantified police dataset with the undercount caveat.

RNZ (27 Feb 2025), Counting Ourselves survey: almost one in five trans and non-binary New Zealanders were threatened with physical violence because of their gender identity in the past four years, and 8% experienced deliberate physical violence — the first clear population picture of violence against these communities. For this record: survey-based prevalence figures.

New Zealand Law Commission Issues Paper 53 'Ia Tangata' (June 2024): a review of the protections in the Human Rights Act 1993 for transgender people, non-binary people and people with innate variations of sex characteristics - official law-reform consultation document.

The Spinoff opinion (2 Jul 2024) by Jennifer Shields: after a spate of rainbow event cancellations and a 2023 Posie Parker protest, calls for more security for rainbow communities — noting statutory wins (Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Act 2021 easing ID correction; Conversion Practices Prohibition Act 2022) alongside a worsening street climate. For this record: community-safety assessment dated mid-2024 with the recent statutory wins named.

Spartacus Gay Travel Index 2026 (Feb 2026): annual index measuring the legal situation and living conditions for queer people in each country across 18 categories (marriage to death penalty); color-coded from dark green (most liberal) to red (most dangerous); explains its rating system including negative points for death-penalty laws and Sharia application.

glbtq encyclopedia entry on New Zealand (Andrew Matzner, 2004): long history of liberal reform (women's suffrage 1893); Gay Liberation Front emerged April 1972; decriminalisation followed years of activism; Georgina Beyer reportedly the first transsexual in the world to achieve national office; 13th country with equal marriage (2013).

PrideNZ.com: archive of over 1,000 audio recordings of interviews and events from Aotearoa NZ's LGBTQIA+ communities, a rainbow timeline, over 18,000 GayNZ.com articles (2001-2017), and Homosexual Law Reform 40th-anniversary resources including Hansard transcripts of the parliamentary debates. For this record: a usable local community/archive resource base (context, not risk).
